episodes.168013: Persistent convection occurred through the day into early evening across the CSRA and western Midlands in a zone of convergence ahead of an approaching shortwave trough. Moderate instability was present with weak wind shear. Only a single damage report occurred with this event.
episodes.168024: An upper low, slowly approaching the region over Missouri, combined with clearing afternoon skies to provide adequate instability, while east-southeasterly surface winds promoted ample low-level wind shear.  Amid this environment, several strong, northward-moving, rotating thunderstorms formed over west-central portions of central Indiana through early evening.  One cell spawned a brief EFU tornado in Montgomery County.
episodes.168071: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours ahead of a slow moving low pressure system.
episodes.168073: Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours as a low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley.
episodes.168078: Strong to locally severe storms developed in a modestly unstable atmosphere, aided by a 50 knot mid level wave. A few marginally severe wind gusts were recorded along with some tree damage in a few locations.
episodes.168189: Thunderstorms produced downburst winds which caused some property damage across areas of Humboldt and Elko Counties.
episodes.168450: Scattered severe thunderstorms moved across parts of southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon and evening of May 25th.
episodes.168451: A brief tornado occurred in northwest Ogle County during the afternoon of May 26th.
episodes.168456: An upper level low pressure system passed east up the Ohio River Valley early on the 27th, resulting in strong south to southeasterly windflow across northwest North Carolina.  A 35-knot low level jet carried deep tropical moisture northward, with precipitable water values rising into the 1.6 to 1.7 inch range along the Blue Ridge in northwest North Carolina.  Orographic lift enhanced rainfall amounts, especially across Watuaga County, where the headwaters of the Watauga River observed totals ranging from 2.5 to 4.0 inches over an 18 to 24 hour period.
episodes.168731: Several rounds of showers and thunderstorms developed across all of eastern Iowa, northwest Illinois and far northeast Missouri on the afternoon of Thursday May 26, 2022. These showers and storms formed in response to an area of low pressure moving across eastern Missouri into central Illinois during the afternoon and evening. This activity slowly rotated around the low, allowing showers and storms to produce torrential rainfall over areas they impacted. During the evening, repeated rounds of showers and storms impacted the city of Danville, IA, and led to flash flooding across the city. Per emergency management, water flowed into homes, apartments, and a school, and washed out several gravel roads on the west side of town. There was an unofficial measured rainfall amount of 9 inches in the city.
episodes.168822: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved in from the south through the morning, resulting in sporadic severe weather reports, especially in counties along the Mississippi River. A few reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received.
episodes.168823: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved in from the south through the morning, resulting in sporadic severe weather reports, especially in counties along the Mississippi River. A few reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received.
episodes.168964: A closed low over the Ohio Valley pushed a warm front into northern North Carolina. Increasing low level shear in this region and modest instability, lead to scattered severe thunderstorms which produced damaging winds and two brief tornadoes.
episodes.169106: A line of isolated thunderstorms developed just south of a nearby warm front just before sunrise. In the presence of sufficient shear and instability, one thunderstorm produced a short-lived tornado that produced minor damage in Colleton County.
episodes.169276: Thunderstorms broke out across east Kentucky May 26th thanks to a mature low pressure system moving into the Ohio Valley from the west. This system initially pulled a warm front through eastern Kentucky in the evening, and most of the severe convection was associated with the approach and passage of this warm front. A cold front was then dragged across the region overnight and into the morning. Instability was not overly impressive going into this event, around 1000-1500 J/kg of CAPE. However, storms that formed were able to take advantage of the roughly 40 kts of effective shear over the area and organize into more multicellular and linear structures. The limited CAPE profile meant a more limited hail threat, leaving strong to damaging wind gusts as the primary threat, though tornadoes were not able to be ruled out. Even though storm motions were fairly swift, given the abundant moisture associated with this system, there was also a threat for flash flooding if any training set up or an area was hit multiple times. Several warnings, including Severe Thunderstorm, Flash Flood, and Tornado, were issued that evening, mainly across our most western and southwestern counties. Multiple reports of damaging wind leading to downed trees were received across the same areas, along with a couple of reports of water flowing over roadways. There were some wind reports within the Tornado Warnings, but no tornadoes were confirmed in the JKL area.
episodes.169358: Multiple rounds of strong to severe storms affected the area with impacts to trees and power lines.  In addition, persistent heavy rain along the coast resulted in flooding in portions of Gulf county with over a foot of rain reported.
episodes.169375: A weak cold front brought a round of strong thunderstorms to the area with a few gusts measured in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.169619: Routed water from heavier early-spring precipitation well to the north brought sections of the James River above flood stage for the first time in nearly two years.
episodes.169683: On the evening of May 26th, a strong cold front was crossing through the Ohio Valley with accompanying showers and thunderstorms passing over eastern Kentucky. One particular storm resulted in a tornado touching down in Greenup County on a hillside south of Little White Oak Road. The tornado tore off a large section of the roof of a home and destroyed the adjacent garage and also caused extensive tree damage as it continued north up a ridge and then onto Cub Run Road.
episodes.169999: A broad band of moderate to heavy rain showers with embedded strong to severe thunderstorms moved over western North Carolina throughout the afternoon into the evening. Several strong to severe thunderstorms produced locally damaging wind gusts, brief large hail, and even a couple of tornadoes, including a strong tornado in Iredell County.
episodes.170025: A broad band of moderate to heavy rain showers with embedded strong to severe thunderstorms moved over upstate South Carolina throughout the afternoon into the evening. A couple of strong to severe thunderstorms produced locally damaging wind gusts and brief large hail.
episodes.170049: Following on the heels of a cold front that moved through the local area on May 25th, yet another cold front came moving through. The LIX sounding showed elevated instability. It was only in the coastal waters where that instability could be utilized by storms. Severe winds were observed at various coastal sites.
episodes.170061: An area of low pressure over north-central Missouri with an associated occluded front arcing southeastward into the Ozarks triggered a band of thunderstorms across central Illinois during the evening of May 25th.  Some of the storms produced wind gusts of around 60mph and isolated wind damage across portions of Morgan, Sangamon, and Logan Counties.
episodes.170062: Low pressure and its associated occluded frontal boundary pushing northeastward out of Missouri triggered a broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms during the afternoon of May 26th.  One cell dropped hail as large as quarters near Marshall in Clark County, while other storms produced winds of 50-60mph and minor wind damage across parts of Clark and Christian Counties.
episodes.170109: The severe weather which moved across central Kentucky during the afternoon and evening hours on May 26th formed thanks to a complex setup involving a nearly stacked surface cyclone located over central Missouri and a cold front which extended across the middle and lower Mississippi valleys. Ahead of the surface front, rich moisture was advected northward from the Gulf of Mexico, helping to destabilize the environment across the region. Multiple broken lines of convection formed in advance of the surface cold front during the early afternoon hours, with embedded strong and severe cells causing wind damage from the Lake Cumberland region up into the Kentucky Bluegrass.
episodes.170219: A TUTT low enhanced the diurnally induced afternoon convection across sections of central and western Puerto Rico between May 23-26. This created long-lasting thunderstorms with periods of heavy rainfall that led to flash flooding and mudslides. Also, the thunderstorms produced small hail and wind damage.
episodes.170248: Slow moving thunderstorms produced isolated flash flooding in Baldwin County.
episodes.170250: Slow moving thunderstorms produced isolated flash flooding in Santa Rosa County.
episodes.170317: Strong thunderstorms moved across the marine area and produced high winds.
episodes.170454: A couple of severe thunderstorms produced 50 knot wind gusts.
episodes.170497: Numerous showers and thunderstorms affected Middle Tennessee on May 25 and again on May 26, mainly during the afternoon hours. Several reports of large hail and wind damage were received.
episodes.170533: A slow moving upper low provided ample tropical moisture over the CWA, with lines of convection forming and pushing SE across the forecast area during the afternoon, with a secondary line forming in the evening along a cold frontal boundary.  The afternoon line of convection produced an isolated severe thunderstorm across central Georgia producing damaging wind reports.

A tornado touched down on the south side of Wilson Mountain Rd just south of the intersection with Key Turney Rd in Falkville, AL. The tornado snapped a couple of hardwood trees and did minor roof damage to a mobile home near its touchdown point. The tornado crossed Wilson Mountain Rd, heading generally in a NE direction and snapped and uprooted trees along its path. One of these hardwood trees fell on a shed at a residence on the north side of Wilson Mountain Rd. A few snapped and uprooted trees were observed along its path as it descended into Devils Cellar Hollow. A couple of large trees were also uprooted to the NE of there along a small section of Jewel Lesalle Ln. This was the last point damage was evident as the tornado moved into rugged, nearly inaccessible terrain. Special thanks to Morgan County, AL EMA for their assistance in this survey.

NWS storm survey found that an EF2 tornado touched down near Tuckers Grove Road in northwest Iredell County and moved northeast. Damage was initially limited to snapped tree limbs and uprooted trees. The tornado intensified as it crossed Bruce Farm Rd, where roof damage occurred to a mobile home and a barn along with continued damage (snapped small-to-medium size trees and uprooted larger trees). One minor injury occurred to a person in the mobile home. The tornado reached its maximum intensity as it continued northeast to Friendship Rd, causing extensive tree damage, including snapped trees. The tornado weakened northeast of this location, snapping tree limbs, uprooting a few trees, and causing minor roof damage to at least one structure before lifting just past Indian Hill Rd.

A National Weather Service survey team inspected storm damage near the community of Buck Shoals and concluded the damage was from an EF-1 tornado. The tornado had max winds around 95 mph with a path length of 1.5 miles. The tornado touched down in a small wooded area just west of Howards Branch Road and proceeded north northeast until lifting along Redbud Lane. Almost all direct damage consisted of numerous mature trees either snapped or uprooted, although one shed was also destroyed.

An EF1 tornado touched down on a hillside south of Little White Oak Road uprooting several trees. The tornado then traveled north across a newly mowed hay field with a convergent pattern evident in the mowed hay, then impacted a house and garage. The tornado tore off a large section of the roof of the home and destroyed the adjacent garage. Residents of the home witnessed the tornado as it was moving across the hay field toward the house and were able to take shelter. The tornado caused additional tree damage as it continued north up a ridge and then onto Cub Run Road.
